It amounted to “simple steps to be ready for everyday emergencies” as part of a wider, community-oriented effort “to improve our resilience as a nation”, he said. Sex, lies and police spies: The disputed story of the ‘creepy’ undercover officer Andrew Coles sings in a church choir, is active in local Conservative politics and was once an undercover Metropolitan Police officer – a so-called “spy cop”. Andrew Coles, pictured with Tory leader Kemi Badenoch, is a former councillor and president of Peterborough Conservative Association Speaking exclusively to the BBC, Coles lists resilience, bravery and ruthlessness as the qualities needed in a good undercover police officer. A skill for deception? “I suppose so,” he says. “Though I didn’t behave very differently to my own personality.” Coles’s current life is a far cry from his covert past when, he says, he sometimes had to break the law to gain trust and maintain his cover. “I took drugs – cannabis. stories.text: CAN ANYONE PLEASE FIND AND UPLOAD THIS DOCUMENTARY? A Prescription for Murder? Panorama Is it possible that a pill prescribed by your doctor can turn you into a killer? Over 40 million prescriptions for SSRI anti-depressants were handed out by doctors last year in the UK. Panorama reveals the devastating side effects on a tiny minority that can lead to psychosis, violence, possibly even murder. With exclusive access to psychiatric reports, court footage and drug company data, reporter Shelley Jofre investigates the mass killings at the 2012 midnight premiere of a Batman movie in Aurora, Colorado. Twenty-four-year-old PhD student James Holmes, who had no record of violence or gun ownership, murdered 12 and injured 70. Did the SSRI anti-depressant he had been prescribed play a part in the killings? Panorama has uncovered other cases of murder and extreme violence which could be linked to psychosis developed after the taking of SSRIs – including a father who strangled his 11-year-old son. Panorama asks if enough is known about this rare side effect, and if doctors are unwittingly prescribing what could be a prescription for murder.

stories.text: RAF Bomber Command 1939 to 1945 documentary – with Dr Robin Clifton of Warwick University. Len Deighton book on history of WW2. Blood, Tears and Folly: An Objective Look at World War II is a 1993 book by Len Deighton is a history of World War II from an alternative viewpoint. Deighton looks for the origins of the war, from the rise of the great power conflicts that led to the First World War, through the inter-war years and the histories of the various conflicts and combatants in the years up until the beginning of the war in 1939. He traces the early engagements, the feints, the so-called Phoney War, right through until Japan’s attack on Pearl Harbor in 1941. Deighton attempts to create an encyclopedic introduction to the conflict by building up a detailed background and showing how perilous Britain’s early situation was, the early blunders by Winston Churchill in the Norwegian Campaign and the British dealings with the French that led to the debacle of Dunkirk. Deighton, a skilled thriller writer, does an exemplary job here of deconstructing the strategy and stupidity of WWII from the British POV. A comparable American-centric work is the ‘Army at Dawn’ trilogy. Nations start wars, and their generals plan battles, often based on wishful thinking instead of facts. When confronted by disaster, they often double-down. As the Allies turn the tide and defeat the Nazis, it is often startling that any success could be achieved. This is the epiphany that Deighton’s work sparks. “Blood, Tears and Folly” is, like Deighton’s other notable non-fiction, about warfare, and the Second World War in particular (with some “setting of the scene” going back thirty or more years in European or world history). His central thesis is that, despite the best efforts of some historians, the actual story of the war in its initial stages is one in which the Allies (the Brits in particular) were overconfident in their ability to respond to the German threat, and in turn doomed themselves to being overrun by the Blitzkrieg of early 1940. No one comes off well here, as Deighton seems to take down many of the mythic figures on the Allied side who have since been revered for their military strength or national importance. This includes Churchill, by the way, and coming from Deighton (as British a writer as you’ll ever find), that says a lot. Do I agree with all of Len’s arguments here? Not necessarily, but I find his writing style entertaining, even when discussing horrible things. And there was a lot of horror during the war, from the obvious widespread murder of the Holocaust and Japanese atrocities in China and elsewhere to the less obvious ones. Deighton can be cranky at times, and I don’t dispute his anger at some of the mistakes as he sees them that unfolded. Overall, I think it’s always best to approach any work of narrative history with a healthy skepticism about the author’s ability to tell the story without leaving something out or being guilty of shaping the tale to fit a narrative. So with that caveat in mind, I think it’s fair to suggest this book as a handy one-volume rundown of some of the war’s less heroic moments, with the understanding that it’s all one man’s perspective. Len Deighton was a wonderful writer, whose fiction has come to mean a lot to me as the last few years have gone by. And this book, which I first attempted to read as a weird teenager during the years when the world seemed to finally be at peace, is a helpful reminder that on the world stage, people fuck it up pretty handily from time to time. The Second World War was a global conflict that didn’t have to happen, if Hitler had been more forcefully opposed and if the Allies hadn’t been more wary of Communism than Fascism. And it could have ended a lot sooner if those same governments had taken the threats seriously or responded more promptly to battlefield outcomes. It really was a war that changed the world, and in “Blood, Folly and Tears,” Len Deighton proves that it was a war that exacted a heavy price for sins of omission and commission on near equal terms.

The Germans will have as big a bill of atrocities against us as we against them If we take them into an impartial international court. there are three further replies which should also be carefully considered by all rational people. In the first place, investigations into the origins of civilian bombing far from the fighting lines (as distinct from the bombing which forms part of a military campaign) make clear the difficulty of justly assessing. wIth who~ lays the fault of starting it. The cumulative growth of ciIvlian bombmg to Its present nightmare stage seems, on present inforrmatlon, to be an outstanding instance of the tragic fashion in which war-time cruelty grows like a snowball by its own momentum once the power of Juggernaut has taken control. Some accidental violatIon of international law, assumed to be deliberate, is repaid by a reprisal in kind . The enemy ‘hits back’; we retaliate harder still; in each case the accidental consequences (such as the bombing of a church in mistake for a factory) are advertised for propaganda purposes by the victim as having been intentional. So the grim competition goes on, until the mass-murder of civilians becomes part of our policy – a descent into barbarism which we should have contemplated with horror in 1939. Secondly, it is a fact – as this book will show – that though parts of Britain suffered cruelly in the Blitz, some of the terrible inventions and tactics now being used were not known or practised at that stage of the War. Even in those early days, the knowledge of our distress and confusion was limited to the areas which endured them, and particularly to the surviving victims and to Civil Defence and rescue workers, who had actually to deal with the shambles to which German bombs reduced many humble homes. It is, I believe, the comparative rarity of first-hand experience among the majority of the British people which accounts for their supine acquiescence of obliteration bombing as a policy.’ My own experience is relatively small, but as a Londoner who has been through about 600 raid periods and has spent 18 months as a volunteer fireguard, I have seen and heard enough to know that I at least must vehemently protest when this obscenity of terror and mutilation is inflicted upon the helpless civilians of another country.’

stories.text: Slaughterhouse 5 novel about the RAF bombing of Dresden. Slaughterhouse-Five, or, The Children’s Crusade: A Duty-Dance with Death is a 1969 semi-autobiographic science fiction-infused anti-war novel by Kurt Vonnegut. It follows the life experiences of Billy Pilgrim, from his early years, to his time as an American soldier and chaplain’s assistant during World War II, to the post-war years. Throughout the novel, Billy frequently travels back and forth through time. The protagonist deals with a temporal crisis as a result of his post-war psychological trauma. The text centers on Billy’s capture by the German Army and his survival of the Allied firebombing of Dresden as a prisoner of war, an experience that Vonnegut endured as an American serviceman. The work has been called an example of “unmatched moral clarity” and “one of the most enduring anti-war novels of all time”. The book has been translated into at least 11 other languages, including German (twice), Italian (twice), French, Polish, Portuguese, Bulgarian, and Chinese. The novel’s first chapter begins with “All this happened, more or less”; this introduction implies that an unreliable narrator tells the story. Vonnegut utilizes a non-linear, non-chronological description of events to reflect Billy Pilgrim’s psychological state. Events become clear through flashbacks and descriptions of time travel experiences. In the first chapter, the narrator describes his writing of the book, his experiences as a University of Chicago anthropology student and a Chicago City News Bureau correspondent, his research on the Children’s Crusade and the history of Dresden, and his visit to Cold War–era Europe with his wartime friend Bernard V. O’Hare. In the second chapter, Vonnegut introduces Billy Pilgrim, an American man from the fictional town of Ilium, New York. Billy believes that an extraterrestrial species from the planet Tralfamadore held him captive in an alien zoo and that he has experienced time travel.

stories.text: BBC 4 Extra – Great Lives – Shirley Williams on her Mum, Vera Brittain. Vera Brittain Great Lives The writer and pacifist Vera Brittain is discussed by her daughter Baroness Shirley Williams and Dr Clare Gerada, Chair of the Royal College of GPs. Vera Brittain’s life was shaped by the grief that followed the loss of her fiance, her brother and two good friends. She candidly conveyed the toll of the First World War on her generation in the best-selling 1933 book, Testament of Youth. Matthew Parris chairs an insightful exploration of what it was like to be brought up by Vera a mother who was, for many reasons, simply unavailable to the young Shirley Williams. Vera was a teenage feminist desperate for an education. But she turned her back on her studies at Oxford in 1914 because she felt compelled to serve as a nurse, wanting to join her brother and his friends in the trenches. Shirley Williams explains that as a result of her experiences, Vera became a committed pacifist, at a time when it was deeply unpopular to do so. Dr Clare Gerada nominates a fascinating life while paying tribute to two women – mother and daughter – who she believes have made the 21st century a better place for women to live. Produced by Mark Smalley. First broadcast on BBC Radio 4 in 2012.

stories.text: ‘It’s a bitter pill to swallow’ – Truth behind King Charles’ £100m taxpayer-funded grant With former Cabinet minister Lord George Foulkes questioning government funding for the monarchy, the Mirror’s Pod Save the King royal YouTube show delves into the debate on public funding for the Firm The monarchy’s expected £100million grant from the taxpayer is a “bitter pill to swallow for a lot of people”, according to the Mirror’s royal editor Russell Myers. It comes as former Cabinet member Lord George Foulkes has argued the public is not getting value for the £100million it is set to hand over next year to fund the royals. . He was expected to say that the funding – known as the sovereign grant – must be revised as Britain endures a lasting cost of living crisis. And on this week’s episode of the Mirror’s award-winning podcast Pod Save the King, the cash for the monarch is discussed and it is questioned if theere should be more transparency on royal finances. Russell told the YouTube show: “How can you sort of sit back and have a man at the top of the shop [King] who is worth £2 billion, and we are still paying for the fuel for their helicopter and for the royal train to leave the station? I think that is a bitter pill to swallow for a lot of people.” The Mirror’s deputy royal editor Jennifer Newton agreed, as she argued that if the monarchy was more forthcoming with their finances, the public would be able to have a more informed opinion about how taxpayer cash is being used. Jennifer explained: “I think if there was more transparency, even if the numbers don’t look particularly good or the optics aren’t good, but at least if they were being a bit more transparent, we could then have a more honest conversation and debate about it.” Russell agreed, saying: “It is a fine balancing act. I understand where Lord is coming from, but it will be very interesting to see if this gains any traction. Because, I mean, I think we are in such a state, not only here but across the world, of this cost of living crisis that is just unending. The £100 million Sovereign Grant covers expenses for the royal’s engagements(Image: WPA Pool, Getty Images) “And how on earth can we keep on funnelling this money? Should the government be putting more pressure, rather than sort of treating the royal family with kid gloves? Are we getting value for money?” Lord Foulkes previously told the Mirror he was incensed by the monarch’s use of private jets and helicopters and questioned why the family needs so many homes while making public statements on homelessness. He was expected to tell peers that the UK has by far the most expensive state-funded monarchy in Europe as he argued the Sovereign Grant is too high. The former Scotland Secretary was to say in his address: “When we ask the public to fund an institution to the tune of over just under £100 million a year through the Sovereign Grant, at a time when many are facing severe pressure on their household budgets, we have a duty to ask two fundamental questions – are we getting value for money, and do the actions of this institution match the values it preaches? I would argue that the answer to both is no.” Lord Foulkes added: “While European neighbours have streamlined their royal houses, we continue to fund a sprawling network of ‘working royals’ whose ribbon-cutting duties would, in any other sector, face strict audit and productivity metrics.” The grant is an annual payment to fund the monarch’s official duties, such as overseas and domestic trips, while also paying for the ongoing £369 million refurbishment of Buckingham Palace. The payment – based on profits from both the Crown Estate and taxpayer funds – also covers the cost of employing staff, upkeep on royal residences around the UK, and hosting official events such as garden parties and state visits. New episodes of the Mirror’s award-winning royal podcast Pod Save The King are available each week on YouTube. stories.subtitle: Why Earl Spencer’s damning memoir rings so true to me… They last met at London’s Tate Gallery on July 1 – Princess Diana’s 36th birthday. It was unexpected.
stories.text: Richard Kay – Mountbatten stopped relationship with John Spencer and Queen. Why Earl Spencer’s damning memoir rings so true to me… They last met at London’s Tate Gallery on July 1 – Princess Diana’s 36th birthday. It was unexpected. ‘Neither of us had any idea that the other was going to be at the evening,’ Charles Spencer observed. Typically, he noted, his sister was not celebrating her special day with friends but was working: guest of honour at a charity fundraiser. They were never to see each other again. Nine weeks later, with Diana dead and a nation convulsed in grief, Earl Spencer was to recall this briefest of final encounters in his powerful eulogy from the pulpit of Westminster Abbey. From time to time Earl Spencer, the baby brother whom Diana had mothered as a child, would speak out against some of the more lurid fantasies. Occasionally he would take aim at the royals too: one year complaining that William and Harry may not have been encouraged to stay in touch with their mother’s side of the family; another, wondering why the then Prince Charles had never visited his ex-wife’s island grave at Althorp, the Spencer family home in Northamptonshire. But mostly he kept quiet, as he and his family tried to hold fast to their memories of the woman to whom he paid such moving tribute. Now, with the 30th anniversary of the princess’s death 11 months away, comes, at last, Charles Spencer’s own brilliant examination of his sister, in order to right some of those wrongs. It is an explosive yet thoughtful book, simply entitled Swan Song. But it is at times unflinching when it comes to Diana in the raw, the sister he so memorably described from the Abbey pulpit as ‘a very British girl who transcended nationality’. It is an insider’s account from the ultimate insider, one of only a handful who knew Diana for almost the entire span of her life. It is elegiac and moving, with childhood memories of growing up with Diana, who was three years his senior. But it is also at times painful, as the rollercoaster of the princess’s life escalated to a whirlwind pace on marrying the heir to the throne. Nor does he shrink from how her celebrity impacted his family – the fallings out and the breakdown in relations. At the time of her death, she had not spoken to their mother for almost four months. And he details his own quarrel with her, when he changed his mind about allowing Diana the use of a property she had her heart set on at the Althorp estate. But for King Charles the memoir is a catastrophe. All his careful efforts to rebuild the affection of a nation that was repelled by his treatment of Diana but has come round in the years since – especially since he assumed the crown – risk being brutally stripped away.

Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, caused a major stir among royal circles after its rather shocking allegations against the King were revealed. The Earl, who vowed this book would be his final, accused the King of being “giddily excited” during a phone call following Princess Diana’s tragic death, and insisted the late princess would be forgotten “soon enough”. The Palace promptly responded with a fiery statement, appearing to echo sentiments said behind the scenes – that King Charles had been left furious. “While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss,” a Buckingham Palace spokesman told GB News. It resulted in an angry response from the Earl, who accused the King of “gaslighting” him. “It was astonishingly provocative and below the belt because it was essentially trying to say I’d lied without the King being able to deny what I’d said,” he declared. Author Andrew Morton, who penned Diana: Her True Story back in 1992, feels the statement was rash and the King “got it wrong”. “With [Earl] Spencer’s book, he, within an hour or so, issued a statement,” he told The Telegraph. “I would have thought that sensible courtiers would have said to him, ‘Hang fast, sir, because it’s only a book – these things will pass.’ “But I think it’s a sign of how angry he was that this statement was written almost contemporaneously, and in a way, it’s a statement written for an audience of one, and that’s King Charles.”…

Mossad interventions in UK. Last March, top national security officials gathered inside the White House to discuss with Mr. Trump how to respond to the nerve agent attack in Britain on Sergei V. Skripal, the former Russian intelligence agent. London was pushing for the White House to expel dozens of suspected Russian operatives, but Mr. Trump was skeptical. He had initially written off the poisoning as part of legitimate spy games, distasteful but within the bounds of espionage. Some officials said they thought that Mr. Trump, who has frequently criticized “rats” and other turncoats, had some sympathy for the Russian government’s going after someone viewed as a traitor. During the discussion, Ms. Haspel, then deputy C.I.A. director, turned toward Mr. Trump. She outlined possible responses in a quiet but firm voice, then leaned forward and told the president that the “strong option” was to expel 60 diplomats. To persuade Mr. Trump, according to people briefed on the conversation, officials including Ms. Haspel also tried to show him that Mr. Skripal and his daughter were not the only victims of Russia’s attack. Ms. Haspel showed pictures the British government had supplied her of young children hospitalized after being sickened by the Novichok nerve agent that poisoned the Skripals. She then showed a photograph of ducks that British officials said were inadvertently killed by the sloppy work of the Russian operatives. Ms Haspel was not the first to use emotional images to appeal to the president, but pairing it with her hard-nosed realism proved effective: Mr. Trump fixated on the pictures of the sickened children and the dead ducks. At the end of the briefing, he embraced the strong option. The outcome was an example, officials said, of how Ms. Haspel is one of the few people who can get Mr. Trump to shift position based on new information. “Her style and the way she projects herself in these kind of senior situations is disarming, without showing weakness,” said Doug Wise, a former C.I.A. officer who has worked with Ms. Haspel.

The Greens Look To Get Serious On The Economy Green Party figures are wrestling with a question: how can they demonstrate economic credibility while maintaining their radical edge? It was a talking point at their conference in Brighton over the weekend. Harriet Lamb, Green Party CEO, told a fringe event hosted by More in Common that looking “competent on the economy” would be important to the party’s next steps as it tries to build on the growth it has achieved since Zack Polanski took over as leader. At the same event, the think tank’s executive director, Luke Tryl, presented data showing that the public views a Green Party focus on the economy almost just as favourably as a focus on the environment. Among a section of avid Green supporters, which More in Common calls Progressive Activists, a focus on the economy is significantly more popular. Senior Green figures who PoliticsHome spoke to in Brighton said the party must prepare for intense media scrutiny of its economic policies in the months ahead – particularly if there is talk of the role the party could play in a coalition government. To that end, the Greens are planning to expand their team of economic spokespeople, with councillors elected in May in the pool of people being considered, PoliticsHome understands. The Secretary of the Greens’ Economy Policy Working Group, Nadine Storey, admitted there is some nervousness within the party about presenting a different economic approach to the Westminster orthodoxy as “you need spokespeople who can defend the policy”. Speaking to PoliticsHome in Brighton, she said: “Zack has been very good at that. “He’s been much bolder, braver at being prepared to take on the journalists, but he has been caught out once or twice because he didn’t know the nitty-gritty.” On Sunday, Green conference voted in favour of a motion setting out what Storey described as “underpinnings” to the party’s radical economic policy. It includes dropping interest rates as the main means of controlling inflation; no longer using Gross Domestic Product as a measure of economic policy success; and abolishing the Office for Budget Responsibility. Party rules mean that the motion is now official policy.

Analysis by the Centre for Social Justice (CSJ) found that a single economically inactive claimant receiving Universal Credit health and housing support alongside Personal Independence Payment can receive approximately £27,400 a year, tax free. A worker would need to earn more than £33,000 before tax to take home the same amount, rising to almost £35,000 if a minimum pension contribution is made. The report, to be published on Tuesday, warns that the rapid growth in mental health-related claims has turned this into a “new benefit trap”. Although claimants can keep some benefits in work, the research corroborates recent findings from the Milburn Review that for young people with a health condition, inactivity can offer “higher income, less hassle and lower risk than trying to find work”. The findings will be published in State of Dependency, a 250-page report and part one of the CSJ’s landmark Welfare 2030 inquiry, chaired by former Work and Pensions Secretary Sir Iain Duncan Smith MP. The report estimates that 6.2 million full-time workers – around one in four – take home less than the combined benefit package. The Government has reduced the Universal Credit health element for most new claims from £429.80 to £217.26 a month, reducing the package to approximately £24,800 a year. The Green Party and Nuclear Energy Christopher Busby The recent Brighton conference policy change of the Green Party of England and Wales to embrace nuclear energy was sad but not unexpected. I have believed since Fukushima that the nuclear operators (which we used to call the nuclear military complex, or their agents, the nuclearists) had started seriously focusing on the last political fortress of those opposing nuclear. In the hysteria following Fukushima, they were forced to bring out their Queen, George Monbiot and his Guardian megaphone. This began with his Pauline conversion (no one has died from the radioactive releases) and moving to his attacks on me, on Christopher Busby (false scientist, fraud). I have written and spoken elsewhere that all that he said about me (peddling anti-radiation pills and making stupid epidemiological mistakes) was a pack of lies and half-truths, supported by bogus scientists like Gerry Thomas so I won’t say any more here about that. Except that the Green Party immediately disowned me, and all the funding I was receiving (Joseph Rowntree Charitable Trust, the Goldsmiths, the Gillettes) vanished. But at the time, I was the Green Party National Speaker on Science and Technology, and immediately following Fukushima, I explained the problem on prime-time TV News for the BBC and also ITN. You can see these interviews on Youtube still. Everything I said then (opposed by some pro-nuclear furby) has since been shown to be true. Cancer and leukemia rates have increased in Japan, and also generally every country that provides cancer data. But the Green Party began as an anti-nuclear party in Germany, with Petra Kelly. When I chained myself to the gates of Trawsfynydd Nuclear Power Station in Wales in 1992, Petra Kelly had agreed to come and support our campaign against opening the nuclear site, which was dangerous. The station operators had applied to run the reactors at a high temperature to anneal the cracks in the pressure vessel. This was not long after the experiment at Chernobyl. And the contamination of Wales by Chernobyl (which led to sharp increases in cancer and child leukemia). The Aftermath: The protest successfully amplified the public safety debate surrounding the station’s embrittled reactor pressure vessels. It is frequently cited by Busby and Green Party organizers as a pivotal moment of non-violent pressure that ultimately pushed the operator to announce the plant’s permanent economic closure the following year. We were all a bit scared by this project. The nuclear police had pistols and we were told they would shoot us. Petra Kelly was assassinated a few months after this. How can I say this? How do I know? Well, of course I don’t know and cannot be sure. But here is something you don’t know about this. The story now widely accepted (look at Wikipedia) is that her man, General Gert Bastiaan killed her. The police determined that Kelly was shot dead while sleeping by Bastian, who then died of suicide. Well and Good. But I spoke with Prof Ernest Sternglass about this. He knew both of them, and said it was impossible that Bastiaan would have killed her and himself. They were full of positive energy and life, when he met them in Berlin some 6 weeks before she died. She was very excited. She had received an offer of considerable financial support by German TV to make a series of documentaries with Russian and Belarussian scientists including Dr. Shevchenko, to report on the real health effects of the Chernobyl accident contamination. At the time, the nuclear operators and their tame scientists in the IAEA and the WHO were stating that there were no measurable health effects. It was the same at Fukushima some twenty years later. But back in those days they killed you, rather than using media to destroy your credibility. Erin Brockovitch for example. Ernest told me he later had a phone call from Shevchenko from Mexico who told him he was on the run and feared for his life.

On a scorching summer’s day we passed healthy looking rows of potatoes, wheat and alliums to cross a field towards a collection of semi hidden structures behind a small, yet productive forest garden. We found Ed picking leaves in his prolific polytunnel. Known as ‘Biochar Ed’ to many, Ed greeted us with his characteristic humility and enthusiasm. A repository of vast amounts of knowledge Ed speaks with an ardent urgency evidenced in the multiple tracks of thoughts that rush out of his brilliant mind. We were soon introduced to one of his inventions – a biochar rocket stove. We had encountered biochar during our time in Costa Rica so it was interesting to see its application in a more familiar setting. Carbon negative cup of tea anyone? Ed’s enthusiasm for biochar is perhaps best explained by the man himself, who, in a three part series for Permaculture Magazine, discusses the creation, and application, of biochar – including his own biochar rocket stove hybrid. “Biochar is charcoal intended to be used as a soil additive rather than to be burnt. There are two main reasons for making and using it: firstly, to improve crop yields by increasing the soil’s nutrient holding capabilities, increasing moisture retention, reducing acidity and influencing the activity of the soil micro organisms; and secondly, to stabilise the carbon in biomass and thereby sequester atmospheric carbon dioxide.” The TLUD stove, where we made all our tea and cooked all our meals (we scratched together handfuls of plentiful woodchip from the nearby polytunnel floor), was a cinch to use. Over the sound of a whirring fan and hum of the brilliant smokeless flame, Ed took us through the mechanics of his outdoor stove. Inspired by the work of Paul Anderson and his work on biochar stoves Ed created his own version which he had recently designed and got working. Made of two chambers in a reused gas cylinder, woodchip is deposited into the inner chamber: a container for a loose bulk material that tapers downward and is able to discharge its contents at the bottom. Air, with the assistance of a battery powered fan, is drawn in as the woodchip is lit from above. Most of the air goes up between the two cylinders and is blown through a ring of holes. The wood gases rise and you get a ring of fire at the top. Because there is not enough air in the retort (the outer chamber) for the combustion of the wood chip, pyrolysis occurs. Failure to activate Hormuz fertilizer plan could trigger food crisis, UN official says BANGKOK, Oct 14 (Reuters) – A failure ?by the United States and Iran to agree within weeks on a UN-backed plan for moving fertilizer through the Strait of Hormuz could cause a ?food security crisis in parts of Asia and Africa, an official overseeing the proposed scheme said on Wednesday. The United Nations set up a taskforce in March to facilitate passage of fertilizers through the strait. It is yet to implement the mechanism it drew up, but United Nations Under-Secretary-General Jorge Moreira da Silva said this could be activated within 7-10 days of an agreement between Washington and Tehran. “It’s absolutely crucial to ‘get the deal in the next few weeks. Otherwise, we will miss the planting season,” he said in an interview in Bangkok, on the sidelines of ?the International Monetary Fund and World Bank annual meetings. In response to questions from Reuters, a US State Department spokesman said the US military ?has assisted thousands of commercial vessels with transiting the strait. “The United States will continue to take decisive action against Iran’s attempts to disrupt freedom of navigation through the Strait ?of Hormuz and hold the global economy hostage,” he said. The White House and Iran’s Embassy in Bangkok did not immediately reply to a request for comment. Iran has sought to tighten ?its grip on the Strait of Hormuz since US and Israeli strikes on February 28, using the chokepoint to pressure Washington, which has been pressing its own naval blockade of Iranian ports. Before the war, the waterway handled roughly a third of globally traded urea — the world’s most widely used fertilizer — and nearly half of seaborne sulphur, a key input. It is also a major conduit for global oil supplies. Fertilizer ?shipments out of the Gulf region remained largely halted more than six months after the start of the conflict, the Washington-based International Food Policy Research Institute said in a note ?last month. Fertilizer products accounted for a “very negligible” share of the resumption of some shipping during a ceasefire between mid-June and mid-July, it said. FIVE VESSELS A DAY If the Hormuz disruption continues, commodity prices could ?rise by ?up to 81% for cereals, 66% for oil crops and 30% for animal products, according to an August report by the International Chamber of Commerce. “If we miss that planting season, the productivity of agriculture would significantly drop and the impact on prices will significantly increase,” said Moreira da Silva, who is also the executive director of the United Nations Office for Project Services. The proposed operation would use a coordination centre in Oman to register vessels and coordinate safe passage, with UN monitors working alongside local authorities at Gulf ports to verify ?cargo loading. The passage of only five vessels ?per day through Hormuz could keep fertilizer ?supplies flowing to countries in critical need, Moreira da Silva said. Ships would be tracked during transit, and additional inspections could be carried out if countries raised concerns about a vessel or its cargo, he added. MULTIPLE SHIPPING CHOKEPOINTS Iran and the United States have exchanged proposals through ?intermediaries since a June interim ceasefire collapsed, but efforts to reopen the Strait of Hormuz have stalled over Tehran’s conditions and ?Washington’s insistence on addressing ?Iran’s nuclear programme from the outset.

The £4m dredging project to remove silt from a city’s docks has begun, but what is the long-term solution to prevent it from returning? Silt levels at Gloucester Docks became so high this summer that water depths fell below navigable levels, leaving boats trapped and forcing the docks to close. The Canal & River Trust (CRT), which manages the Gloucester and Sharpness Canal, began dredging on Monday, with the work costing the trust about half of its total dredging budget. But Gloucester MP Alex McIntyre said this was only a short-term solution, adding: “We are going to keep seeing this problem as climate change gets worse.” The silt has become visible in Gloucester Docks in recent weeks, forcing it close What is causing the silt? Silt typically enters Gloucester Docks because water has to be pumped from the River Severn into the canal to keep it functioning. During long periods of dry weather, lower river levels can mean water is drawn from areas closer to the riverbed, where the concentration of sediment is often higher. This can result in more silt entering the system. There has also been speculation that the build-up of silt has been made worse due to water being pumped from the Gloucester and Sharpness Canal to supply drinking water to people in Bristol. There has been a long-term agreement since the 1960s to supply water to Bristol from the canal. This has led to some to question if Bristol Water stopped this process, would CRT not need to pump as much water, and therefore silt, from the River Severn?

New analysis published by the Resolution Foundation discovered the past five years of a near-continuous cost of living pressures have caused real incomes to drop by almost 8%. The report assesses the toll of three crises – the aftermath of the Covid crisis, the invasion of Ukraine, and conflict in the Middle East – during which inflation peaked at 11.1%. It says energy has been at the “epicentre” of a price shock for households. Higher energy costs have bled into other prices, with food inflation peaking at nearly 20% in March 2023. The pain felt from these price rises has not been shared equally, the think tank found. Inflation was steepest for essentials, which make up a larger share of poorer households’ spending. As a result, the rise in non-housing costs since before the pandemic has been around one-sixth bigger for the poorest tenth of households than for the richest tenth, the report concluded. Overall, it says that the real income of a typical working-age household this year is £2,900 a year lower than they would have been compared to a world in which inflation had stayed at 2% over the past five years. What is RAF Molesworth — and why does it matter? RAF Molesworth is a non-flying military installation in Cambridgeshire, about 70 miles north of London, managed by the United States Air Force. Fox News and the NY Post report it is run by the USAF’s 423rd Air Base Group; its mission is joint intelligence and command operations rather than flying operations. The base hosts intelligence elements for US European Command (EUCOM) and US Africa Command (AFRICOM), plus the NATO Intelligence Fusion Centre — a multinational unit that supplies intelligence to the Supreme Allied Commander Europe (SACEUR). The Straits Times reports the Fusion Centre’s workforce numbers more than 200 personnel, drawing on alliance-wide staff. Molesworth is also the site of a major US intelligence construction project. The Joint Intelligence Analysis Complex (JIAC) is a $556.5 million project, according to the US Defense Visual Information Distribution Service, which held its groundbreaking ceremony at RAF Molesworth on April 12, 2024. The facility consolidates around 1,700 intelligence personnel from roughly 20 facilities as part of the US European Infrastructure Consolidation programme, with construction expected to take about four years. The site’s history goes back further: Fox News notes the airfield was used by US bombers in the Second World War and deactivated in 1973, while The Hindu reports the RAF founded the station in 1917. Few UK installations carry comparable sensitivity today — which is why a fence-cutting intrusion at 2 a.m. has drawn a counter-terrorism response. Who are the two Latvian men arrested at RAF Molesworth, and are they spies? Their names have not been published. Police describe them as Latvian nationals resident in the UK, reported as aged 32 and 36. They were arrested on suspicion of national-security offences under Section 4 of the National Security Act 2023 — which covers entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK — but they have not been charged, and the motive for the intrusion is unknown. It is too early, and wrong, to characterise them as spies. What is RAF Molesworth and why is it so important to US and NATO intelligence? RAF Molesworth is a non-flying US Air Force installation in Cambridgeshire, about 70 miles north of London. It hosts intelligence elements for US European Command and US Africa Command, plus the NATO Intelligence Fusion Centre, which supplies intelligence to NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe. A $556.5 million Joint Intelligence Analysis Complex is under construction there to consolidate around 1,700 US intelligence personnel from about 20 facilities. Is the RAF Molesworth break-in connected to the RAF Fairford terror plot? stories.text: Live streaming of US death penalty.‘Medieval’ and ‘disturbing’: US plan to livestream execution elicits global condemnation Pentagon said execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, who killed 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009, would be broadcast live The US is facing worldwide condemnation over a “barbaric” plan to execute a disabled man by firing squad and livestream it to the public, with critics comparing the Trump administration to dictatorships in Iran and Afghanistan. The Pentagon confirmed on Thursday that the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, convicted of killing 13 people at a military base at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009, would be livestreamed on 3 December. The United Nations’ office of the high commissioner for human rights warned on Friday that broadcasting the killing would amount to a public execution and “breach the absolute prohibition of torture”. The plan also drew opprobrium from politicians, religious leaders and human rights advocates in the US and abroad. Hillary Clinton, the former US secretary of state, wrote on social media: “A barbaric idea, beneath our dignity as a country. Push back on this.” Yassamin Ansari, the first Iranian American Democrat elected to the US Congress, posted: “In Trump’s America, we’re doing public executions now. WTF. This is what happens under brutal dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan. It’s all part of Trump’s authoritarian takeover of the United States.” Britain, which abolished the death penalty in the 1960s, moved to distance itself from the execution. Bridget Phillipson, the UK’s equalities minister and Labour party chair, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme that she found the concept “rather disturbing”. Phillipson stressed that the decision was a matter for the US government, adding: “They are a close ally. Does that mean that we support everything the US government does? No.” Under US military law, a president must approve an execution by firing squad. Trump did so on the recommendation of his defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, according to the Pentagon. JD Vance – a practicing Catholic – told reporters on Friday he wouldn’t watch the livestreamed execution of Hasan, but stopped short of criticizing the administration’s decision. When asked how his Christian beliefs influence his view of the public execution, Vance dismissed controversy about the manner of execution and appeared to question whether the livestream will happen. “Whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope the people don’t forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people,” the US vice-president told reporters. “That said, if it’s ultimately livestreamed, I’m not going to be watching it.” Hegseth gleefully confirmed the livestream plan after previously saying that the execution would be public. Speaking to the conservative broadcaster Real America’s Voice, he said people should be able to watch because they need to understand that there were “serious consequences” for such crimes. Asked whether Hasan had made any final requests, Hegseth replied: “Don’t care. We’ll see him on December 3.” Now 56, Hasan was sentenced to death by a military jury in 2013 after being convicted of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted premeditated murder. Twelve of those killed and 30 of the wounded were soldiers. The former army psychiatrist opened fire with a handgun at a medical facility at Fort Hood on 5 November 2009 as soldiers waited for medical checks before deployment. He was shot by a police officer during his arrest and left partly paralysed, and now uses a wheelchair.

stories.text: Tony’s two WWII Bomber Command uncles were Lancaster aircrew bombing Germany in WW2 – with the older brother dying after only 7 bombing raids. 40% of all heavy bomber crews died. Tony has been in Lancashire and Lincolnshire this week visiting museums and airfields, with another newly discovered nephew, Gordon, relating to his uncles. International Bomber Command Centre in Lincoln: start of World War II in September 1939, it had only 280 twin-engined aircraft, 23 operational squadrons and just 15,000 personnel. As the war progressed, however, the addition of heavy aircraft, including the Avro Lancaster, combined with increased scope and manpower, led to it taking a pivotal role in some of the longest and most expensive campaigns of the war . By September 1944, around a quarter of a million men and women were putting over 1,600 aircraft in the air every night, in an effort to bring the war to an end. KEY FACTS Almost a million men and women served or supported Bomber Command during WWII Over 55,500 men from Bomber Command died in the skies over Europe Only 30% of those that flew reached the end of WWII without being killed, injured or taken Prisoner of War Bomber Command crews came from over 60 different countries and it was common to have squadrons and crews comprising numerous nationalities Every member was a volunteer The average age at death was 23. The loss of life was enormous and replacement aircrew, from more than 60 countries across the world and from all walks of life, were continually recruited and trained to help keep Bomber Command in the air. They were all volunteers and most came from across the Commonwealth and occupied Europe, even Germany, having escaped the Nazi regime. As the war progressed, members of the Air Forces of Poland, Canada, Australia and New Zealand all joined the bomber crews. International Bomber Command Centre In May 1940, a highly controversial ‘Area Bombing Directive’ was authorised by Churchill’s Cabinet and Bomber Command began to fly campaigns against the German Navy, the industries of the Ruhr Valley, various German cities, and V1 and V2 missile launch sites, such as at Peenemünde. To carry out this new mandate, additional RAF stations were built all over the UK, each with the population of a large village, and a new Commander-in-Chief was appointed for Bomber Command, Air Marshal Arthur ‘Bomber’ Harris. He promised to make the German people ‘reap the whirlwind’ and this pledge resonated with a desire to strike back at the mighty Nazi war machine. Harris firmly believed that with improved aircraft, such as the Lancaster and Halifax, better training and navigational aids, combined with a renewed will to attack, Bomber Command could knock Germany out of the war. In May 1942, Harris launched his first ‘thousand-bomber raid’ against Cologne. A year later, the famous ‘Dambusters’ raid by 617 Squadron on the dams surrounding the Ruhr Valley, proved that precision strikes were now feasible with modern four-engine bombers and new tactics. Aerial bombing had become a crucial weapon of war, and Bomber Command’s crews and support staff were playing a vital role in ensuring that Nazi Germany’s military machine was severely weakened, by disrupting its workforce and capacity to produce more weapons. International Bomber Command Centre The losses to RAF Bomber Command were also devastating. During 9,111 sorties against Berlin, which often involved return trips of more than 1,000 nautical miles, 492 aircraft were lost and 954 damaged or written off, with more than 3,500 Bomber Command crew members killed or captured during the Battle of Berlin alone…

stories.text: Did the bombing help us win the war or was the killing of so many civilians a misuse of valuable resources? Bishop George Bell opposing the bombing in the House of Lords in 1944. The Area Bombing Directive and Baron Cherwell’s ‘policy of ‘Dehousing’, a military strategy to bomb German civilians which ended up having little effect on either morale or the war. The Butt Report, released on 18 August 1941, was a report prepared during World War II, revealing the widespread failure of RAF Bomber Command aircraft to hit their targets. Any examination of night photographs taken during night bombing in June and July points to the following conclusions: Of those aircraft recorded as attacking their target, only one in three struck within 5 mi (8.0 km). Over the French ports, the proportion was two in three; over Germany as a whole, the proportion was one in four; over the Ruhr it was only one in ten. In the full moon, the proportion was two in five; in the new moon it was only one in fifteen. … All these figures relate only to aircraft recorded as attacking the target; the proportion of the total sorties which reached within 5 miles is less than one-third. … The conclusion seems to follow that only about one-third of aircraft claiming to reach their target actually reached it. Postwar studies confirmed Butt’s assessment, showing that 49% of Bomber Command bombs dropped between May 1940 and May 1941 fell in open country. As Butt did not include those aircraft that did not bomb because of equipment failure, enemy action, weather or which failed to find the target, only about 5% of bombers setting out bombed within 5 mi (8.0 km) of the target. The truth about the failure of Bomber Command shook everyone. Senior RAF commanders argued that the Butt report’s statistics were faulty and commissioned another report, which was delivered by the Directorate of Bombing Operations on 22 September 1941; extrapolating from an analysis of the bomb damage inflicted on British cities, it calculated that the RAF could destroy the forty-three German towns with a population of more than 100,000 using a force of 4,000 bombers. The Chief of the Air Staff, Sir Charles Portal, argued that with such a force Bomber Command could win the war in six months. Not all were convinced and when Churchill expressed his doubts, the Air Staff retrenched and said that even if it did not knock Germany out of the war, it would weaken them sufficiently to allow British armed forces back into Europe. With this compromise between the armed services, Bomber Command was allowed to keep its planned allocation of materiel. This did not stop those outside the Chiefs of Staff questioning the strategic bombing policy…

stories.text: Barf is restoring a former RAF Lightning jet fighter at the former RAF Binbrook airfield where there is also a WWII memorial garden to 460 Sqn RAAF and others who served there. Over the past two years, thanks to continued support from our donors and volunteers, we have successfully run XR724’s No.1 (lower) engine on around six occasions. Each run allowed us to identify and resolve minor issues, steadily improving reliability. Today, the No.1 engine is performing reliably and has been run at several public events—creating memorable experiences for visitors and supporters alike. Over the winter months, attention has turned to the No.2 (upper) engine. Using the same careful, step-by-step approach, work is progressing well, with the aim of demonstrating this engine to the public in the near future. Our annual Open Day will take place on 5th September, and we look forward to welcoming supporters once again. – On a grey day on the Windy Hill, ‘724 broke cloud to the north and flew down the Binbrook runway at approximately 1340 hrs and, after doing flypasts at Scampton, Waddington, Wattisham and Coningsby, touched down at the spiritual home of the Lightning in front of an enormous crowd and shut down its engines after back-tracking down the runway to taxy back to the ASF pan past the old Bomb Dump and into the 5 Sqn line, where it was received by Phil Wallis, Mick Cameron and Geoff Commins. We had taken a dead shell and returned it to life and to the air, proving that it was possible for a group of professional engineers to come together from their various occupations and prepare an aircraft of this complexity for flight, to the complete satisfaction of the Design Authority and the engine manufacturer. OK, so ‘724 has flown in and we are in the same position as other groups who got theirs direct, even though it was only after achievements which, we think it is fair to say, many could only have dreamed of. Wrong! We were for a short time, but the ejection seat had to go back and, more importantly, Barry decided he wanted his engines back. That was all fair enough as far as it went, but Barry also decided that he wanted our jet pipes on loan, which he said were now ‘matched’ to his engines and would make the task of getting his own aeroplane flying much easier. We don’t know whether or not that was a fairy story – perhaps some of the engineers out there can tell us – but as he had given us so much help we drew up a proper loan agreement which was signed and witnessed and gave permission for him to take the jet pipes as well. Unfortunately, and unknown to us at the time, he also asked to borrow, and was given by one of our engineering team, the Form 700, which he said would be good evidence of his competence to place before the CAA. Why a photocopy would not have sufficed we don’t know, but as said, it happened without Charles’s knowledge. The jet pipes had been fitted brand new just before ‘724 left Warton to fly into Shawbury and were without doubt the lowest-houred, documented jet pipes in existence. Once safely back at Exeter, however, Barry then told us that unless we paid his CAA costs for the flight that never happened, we would not get the jet pipes and Form 700 back, and since that was financially impossible, we never did. Those jet pipes went out to South Africa and Barry probably still has the Form 700 to this day. As said about Pover before, all this is fully documented in past issues of the Lightning Review and is all in the public domain. So, once again we had a dead jet, but only temporarily. Cutting a long and fraught story short, Charles found and purchased a complete ejection seat with his own money, and this was duly installed. He also managed to successfully tender for three air-lifed and documented engines in an MoD disposal sale, and when we got them back to Binbrook, two were installed in ‘724 and one is still here at Binbrook in its box untouched. We also eventually managed to source the necessary jet pipes, and these were also installed to finally bring ‘724 back to life. It wasn’t easy and it wasn’t cheap, but we did it. For many years after that, the aeroplane was run regularly, and the annual Lightning Rally was held and was the high spot of the year for many members. Unfortunately, since then we have had many problems, not least of which has been the fact that the part of Binbrook where we are has been sold on several times and on each occasion we have had to negotiate the sometimes difficult task of establishing relationships with new owners. But we now find ourselves in a very good situation with a well-stocked and experienced engineering team plus ‘724 undercover for the first time in many years. The future of ‘724 looks bright.

Vera Brittain opposed the bombings – her poem. After a fall in 1966 Vera was never really well again, and in 1970 she died. A memorial service was held for her at St Martin-in-the-Fields, crowded with family, friends, and people from all the organisations she had worked with and for. Her daughter said that when Vera died ‘she believed that as a writer she had been forgotten, the fading voice of a dying generation’. Vera Brittain was the sort of person who acted on her principles as well as talking about them. By 1938 she was publicly protesting against the treatment of Jews in Germany and finding ways to help refugees escape to Britain. When the Second World War began she gave up time and energy to help people whose homes had been bombed. She worked very hard for the PPU’s food relief campaign, set up to help the starving peoples of occupied Europe. This was a project that proved controversial, as some people believed that such aid would make the war last longer, and others thought it would help ‘the enemy’. But Vera saw this work as a practical way of being a pacifist: helping to ease the suffering caused by war. Above all, she believed that people should know the truth about what was happening. From 1940 to 1946, she produced her fortnightly ‘Letter to Peace-lovers’, which gained 2,000 subscribers (some of them in the armed forces) and provided them with all the reliable information she could obtain. The government acknowledged that Vera Brittain’s ‘Letters’ were one of the most successful anti-war publications – and she was blacklisted and restricted from travel as a result. (This meant that she couldn’t visit her much-missed children in America.) Vera spent most of the war in London, enduring like everyone else the disruption, food shortages, air raids, exhaustion, anxiety, and lack of sleep. She also visited PPU groups around the country, especially those in devastated cities such as Coventry and Plymouth. Perhaps her experiences of bombing gave her even more inspiration as she embarked on her most famous, and most controversial, campaign. This was against ‘saturation bombing’: the wholesale bombardment of German cities in order to destroy them, civilian populations and all, as a way of forcing the Nazi government to give in. Vera was an active member of the Bombing Restriction Committee, set up in 1942, the year in which RAF fighting policy was changed from ‘precision bombing’ to ‘area bombing’. In one of her Letters, Vera said the British should decide whether ‘we want the government to continue to carry out, through its Bomber Command, a policy of murder and massacre’ in our name. Has any nation the right to make its young men the instruments of such a policy?’ In 1944 she published her book ‘Seed of Chaos: What Mass Bombing Really Means’, in which she provided eye-witness reports of its effects. She vividly pressed home her argument: there was no evidence that the war would be shortened by such destruction – in fact its victims were more likely to want revenge. In any case, if the military intention was to limit slaughter and destruction by bringing the war to a quick end, it was senseless and illogical to try to do it by adding yet more slaughter and destruction to the already horrifying toll The response to ‘Seed of Chaos’ in Britain and America was immediate: Vera became the focus of a rising tide of anger and abuse. With characteristic spirit she said: ‘when people abuse you and defend themselves, you know you have got under their skin and uncovered a bad conscience!’ But as pacifists have discovered throughout their history, their views may also be heard and praised, and sometimes by unlikely listeners. One military expert wrote to Vera to tell her of his ‘profound respect for your courage in upholding claims for human decency in a time when war fever is raging’. Her work did not end with the war. Vera was one of the first people to point out publicly that it was unjust for the whole German nation to be collectively punished for Nazism: after all, many German non-Jews had protested against the regime and had also been sent to the concentration- and death-camps. She also showed how the Nazis’ worst crimes against humanity had actually been made possible by the war. (It was discovered that Vera, too, had been unpopular with the Nazis – whom her abusers had accused her and other pacifists of supporting. Her name had been entered in the Gestapo’s ‘Black Book’, which listed 2,820 people to be arrested at once if Britain was successfully invaded. Pacifism was seen by the Nazis as a very real threat. Vera continued to work for the PPU, and was its chairperson from 1948 until 1951. At this point (she was now approaching 60) she felt she had done all she could for ‘organised’ peace work. Now, with ‘the same principles but different approaches’ she wanted to return single-mindedly to writing. Her ‘Testament of Experience’, describing her life – and her work for peace – was published in 1957. She also continued to write articles about major issues, and she was a regular contributor to ‘Peace News’, the magazine founded by the PPU. She wrote in support of such ideas and projects as the Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament; independence for colonised countries; the anti-apartheid movement in South Africa (‘Peace News’ was banned in South Africa as a result); and political nonviolent protest as taught by Gandhi in India….

Naked statue of Trump named ‘Orange Plague’ unveiled at European Parliament The creator of the sculpture said it was a ‘satirical outcry’ against Trump’s volatile climate and foreign policies A gold statue depicting Donald Trump fully naked and perched on the shoulders of a much smaller man has been unveiled in the European Parliament building in Strasbourg. The eight-foot installation, titled The Orange Plague, is designed by Danish sculptor Jens Galschiøt and covered entirely in 23-karat gold leaf. Trump is shown holding a golf club and a world-shaped ball in one hand and a set of scales in the other. Showing him naked and balanced atop a far smaller man, the statue labels the US president “The King of Injustice” open image in gallery Inscribed on the base is a satirical pledge attributed to “The King of Injustice”. It reads: “I am sitting on the back of a man. He is sinking under my burden. I will do anything to help him. Except stepping down from his back.” Galschiøt, who is known for his politically charged sculptures, has framed the installation as a “satirical outcry” against the volatility of America’s green and foreign policy. “Trump represents one of the greatest threats to the rule-based world order, democratic values, and our common effort to solving the climate crisis,” he said in a statement. “We must address this issue and stand together against such destructive influence.” The sculpture reimagines the artist’s earlier work Survival of the Fattest that shows a starved boy carrying an overweight woman as a visual metaphor for global inequality. Danish MEP Per Clausen commended the unveiling of the new statue, saying: “If someone is so thin-skinned that they cannot tolerate this sculpture being exhibited in the European Parliament, then they have no place on the world stage.” But this is not the first nude effigie of Trump. The latest portrayal of the American president is scheduled to remain in Strasbourg through to Thursday. It is expected to be seen again in November at the UN COP31 Climate Conference in Turkey, where Galschiøt will distribute 3D-printed miniature replicas to delegates.

AUGUST 1914 God said, “Men have forgotten Me; The souls that sleep shall wake again, And blinded eyes must learn to see.” So since redemption comes through pain He smote the earth with chastening rod, And brought Destruction’s lurid reign; But where His desolation trod The people in their agony Despairing cried, “There is no God.” ST. PANCRAS STATION, AUGUST 1915 One long, sweet kiss pressed close upon my lips, One moment’s rest on your swift-beating heart, And all was over, for the hour had come For us to part. A sudden forward motion of the train, The world grown dark although the sun still shone, One last blurred look through aching tear-dimmed eyes— And you were gone. TO A FALLEN IDOL O you who sought to rend the stars from Heaven But rent instead your too-ambitious heart, Know that with those to whom Love’s joy is given You have not, nor can ever have, a part. A nation’s loyalty might have been your glory, And men have blessed your name from shore to shore, But you have set the seal upon your story, And must go hence, alone for evermore. TO MONSEIGNEUR (R.A.L., Lieutenant, Worcesters) None shall dispute Your kingship, nor declare Another could have held the place You hold, For though he brought me finer gifts than gold, And laid before my feet his heart made bare Of all but love for me, and sighed despair If I but feigned my favours to withhold, And would repudiate as sadly cold The proud and lofty manner that You wear, He would not be my pure and stainless knight Of heart without reproach or hint of fear, Who walks unscathed amid War’s sordid ways By base desire or bloodshed’s grim delight, But ever holds his hero’s honour dear— Roland of Roncesvalles in modern days. 1st London General Hospital, November 1915. THE ONLY SON The storm beats loud, and you are far away, The night is wild, On distant fields of battle breaks the day, My little child? I sought to shield you from the least of ills In bygone years, I soothed with dreams of manhood’s far-off hills Your baby fears, But could not save you from the shock of strife; With radiant eyes You seized the sword and in the path of Life You sought your prize. The tempests rage, but you are fast asleep; Though winds be wild They cannot break your endless slumbers deep, My little child…

All the ingredients of a typical Northern Ireland crisis have been in place for the past week except for one – violence. A stand-off – over a proposed Orange Order parade in Portadown, opposed by nationalist residents of the Garvaghy Road – has lasted since Sunday morning. Verbal clashes between politicians, late-night negotiations, appeals for calm and a major security operation have all been in the mix. However, the Drumcree parade dispute in Portadown has not descended into disorder or trouble on the streets. Sometimes in Northern Ireland, the definition of success is “nobody got hurt”. The crisis is not over, and fears of an outbreak of street violence remain, but everything is under control at the moment. The truth is few predicted a relatively peaceful week when the crisis first erupted. It was an extraordinary seven days. Tension started to build after the Parades Commission, which regulates marches, gave the go-ahead for the controversial Orange Order parade in Portadown to pass along the mainly-nationalist Garvaghy Road. That was on a Friday afternoon. Members of the Orange Order march from Drumcree Church. They are wearing Orange sashes, one person in front is holding a Portadown District banner. The church is in the background. The is the corner of a PSNI Land Rover to the bottom left. Within 24 hours the issue was being battled out at the High Court in Belfast during an urgent Saturday hearing which ended up lasting more than 13 hours.. Sitting under the same roof were those involved in the dispute – Portadown Orange Order and the Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition – headed by Nigel Dawson and Breandán Mac Cionnaith respectively. They sat within a matter of feet from each other but their positions were worlds apart. Court proceedings ended in the early hours of Sunday morning, with the parade given the go-ahead. All involved then made the 30-mile journey through the night from Belfast to Portadown ahead of the scheduled start to the Orange parade at 08:00 BST. By that stage, their route along the Garvaghy Road had been blocked. Up to 1,000 people were standing in the middle of the road, many of them linking arms. stories.text: Theobald Wolfe Tone (Irish: Bhulbh Teón; 20 June 1763 – 19 November 1798), posthumously known as Wolfe Tone, was a revolutionary exponent of Irish independence and is an iconic figure for Irish republicanism. Convinced that if his fellow Protestants feared to make common cause with the Catholic majority, the British Crown would continue to govern Ireland in the English interest, he helped form the Society of United Irishmen in 1791. Fuelled by the popular grievances of rents, tithes and taxes, driven by martial-law repression, and despairing of reform, the society developed as an insurrectionary movement. When in the early summer of 1798 it broke into open rebellion, Tone was in exile soliciting assistance from the French Republic. In October 1798, on his second attempt to land in Ireland with French troops and supplies, he was taken prisoner. Sentenced to be hanged, he died from a reportedly self-inflicted wound. Since the mid-19th century, his name has been invoked, and his legacy disputed, by different factions of Irish republicanism. These have held annual, but separate, commemorations at his graveside in Bodenstown, County Kildare. Society of United Irishmen The Society of United Irishmen was a blood-oath-sworn association, or cult, formed in the wake of the French Revolution, to secure representative government in Ireland. Despairing of constitutional reform, and in defiance both of British Crown forces and of Irish sectarian division, in 1798 the United Irishmen instigated a republican rebellion. Their suppression was a prelude to the abolition of the Irish Parliament in Dublin and to Ireland’s incorporation in a United Kingdom with Great Britain. Espousing principles they believed had been vindicated by American independence and by the French Declaration of the Rights of Man, the Presbyterian merchants who formed the first United society in Belfast in 1791 vowed to make common cause with their Catholic-majority fellow countrymen. Their “cordial union” would upend the landed Anglican Ascendancy and hold government accountable to a reformed Parliament. As it radiated out from Belfast and from Dublin, the society drew on the structure and ritual of freemasonry to recruit among tradesmen, artisans and tenant farmers, many of whom had been organised in their own clubs and secret fraternities. Following its proscription in 1794, its goals were restated in uncompromising terms. Catholic emancipation and parliamentary reform became the call for universal manhood suffrage and a republic. Sharing a common democratic programme, and trading on the prospect of French assistance, agents were active in organising “United” societies in Scotland and in England with whom it was hoped action might be co-ordinated. Beginning in May 1798, martial-law seizures and arrests forced the conspiracy in Ireland into the open. The result was a series of local risings suppressed in advance of the landing, in August, of a small French expeditionary force. In the wake of the rebellion, the British government pressed a union with Great Britain upon the Irish Parliament and transferred its unreformed, exclusively Protestant, representation to Westminster. In 1803, a renewed republican conspiracy, organised on strictly military lines, failed to elicit a response in what had been the United heartlands in the north, and misfired with an aborted rising in Dublin. Exiles formed a United Irish society in the United States where, during the Quasi War with France, it attracted the hostile attention of the governing Federalist Party. There were reports of United Irish oath-taking as a prelude to mutinies in the British Navy, and in Newfoundland and New South Wales. Since the rebellion’s centenary in 1898, Ireland’s major political traditions, unionist, nationalist and republican, have claimed and disputed the legacy of the United Irishmen, and of the union they sought to effect between Catholic, Protestant and Dissenter…

stories.text: The Fairford Fiasco: Unauthorised version. Rather than abandoning the plainly nuts Fairford narrative, Burnham and his government are doubling down on the claim it is an Iranian terror plot. It remains quite possible the men were indeed fuel thieves, simply stealing fuel from farms. They appear to have been equipped for fuel theft and all they were carrying was petrol. It is worth a footnote that there is a very real history of US military personnel, and indeed British personnel, selling military fuel from bases. Stolen red diesel meant for HMS Bulwark fuelled fairground rides throughout England, which I think is rather lovely. But if the Fairford Five were fuel thieves, farms are more probable as the target. We should pause here to acknowledge that USAF Fairford is falsely designated RAF Fairford, itself a propaganda lie, just like “RAF Lakenheath” or “RAF Mildenhall”. The UK is full of US military bases, on which US law applies. (My birth certificate gives my father’s occupation as “Clerk USAF”. He was employed at Mildenhall at the time). It is a classic example of state propaganda that the petrol discovered in the Fairford vans was described by counter terror police as a potential accelerant for a bomb. Well yes, petrol is that. It has however, rather more obvious uses too. The same technique was used at the height of the War on Terror propaganda in the Great Easter Bomb Plot, that never was. Police rounded up and arrested many young Muslims across the Manchester region, which was front-page news. They were all later released without charge. But at the time of arrest the police announced they had found a potential bomb-making ingredient in a kitchen. Well, they had. It was a bag of sugar. Sugar is indeed a potential bomb-making ingredient. Yet most of us have a bag in the kitchen. At least it did not take the police ten days to find the bag of sugar in the kitchen, unlike when they searched Charlie Rowley’s flat for a vial of novichok, and it took them ten days to “find” a bottle of perfume sitting on the kitchen counter. For Fairford, on balance I think a false flag gone wrong is a little more likely than just fuel thieves. We know the men had no bombs and no guns, which makes the terrorist narrative rather hard for the government to sustain. But if they were patsies set up in a false flag, there would be plenty of things already on the base that go bang which could have been used to create the “terrorist incident” around them. Two key points make me think this was a false flag. Firstly the lady farmer who called 999 was adamant there were more men that the five arrested and bailed. The others would have been the spycops – agents provocateurs – who would have been quietly spirited away from the scene. That also fits with the released information that it was one of the men who phoned in a warning about the “attack”. It looks to me like a false flag spectacular had been planned, with US involvement as claimed by Trump and possibly Israeli knowledge as claimed by Netanyahu. This operation by the security services was viewed as over the pay grade of local police (who might be inconveniently honest) who were not in the picture. It all went horribly wrong for the government when an alert local farmer called the local police, and when a participant also called it in. That could have been one of the recruited “terrorists” who got cold feet, or one of the agents panicked they had lost contact with their line of command.

Boeing 737 MAX & Beyond: The Safety Scandals That Forced Aviation To Change In recent history, one of the largest scandals within the aviation industry was that of the cover-up of the MCAS software by American manufacturer, Boeing, on its 737 MAX aircraft. While it initially went unnoticed, the spotlight quickly shone on the aircraft and its systems after two crashes of a similar nature occurred within a few months. This then led to a worldwide grounding of the aircraft type for nearly two years, during which extensive investigations were conducted. While the aircraft type is now considered safe and has been flying for several years, the above-mentioned accidents and several subsequent incidents, along with investigation findings, served as an eye-opening reminder to manufacturers and aviation regulators worldwide that safety should always be a priority. The 737 MAX entered commercial service in 2017 as the next evolution of the manufacturer’s extremely successful aircraft series. While the MAX family was popular and generated significant orders for its various variants, things took a downturn when the entire MAX family was grounded globally for 20 months following two fatal accidents of a similar naturewithin a span of six months. Lion Air Flight 610 (October 2018) This first accident occurred just 12 minutes after a 737 MAX 8 departed from Jakarta, Indonesia, when the aircraft performed an unprompted nose-dive, from which the crew could not recover aircraft control, leading to the unfortunate death of 189 people onboard the aircraft. Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302 (March 2019) This second accident occurred a mere six minutes after departure from Addis Ababa, when the aircraft, also a MAX 8, experienced unstable vertical speed readings, resulting in a similar aircraft reaction to that of the aircraft involved in the Lion Air accident. This led to the unfortunate death of 157 people onboard the aircraft. After the second crash of a similar nature, the industry was quick to react, with regulators worldwide grounding the aircraft type, including the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issuing an Airworthiness Directive (AD) regarding the aircraft family. MCAS Software And Its Cover-Up The findings from these two crashes indicated that the MCAS system onboard the aircraft did not operate as intended. It is essentially software incorporated into the aircraft to offset the nose-up moment inherent in the aircraft design, due to newer, larger engines being placed farther forwardon the wing, which affects the aircraft’s moments about its center of gravity. The software was designed to initiate a “controlled” pitch-down moment and prevent a stall from a significant pitch-up moment caused by engine thrust. Findings from the investigation revealed that the system acted erroneously, forcing the aircraft to pitch down during its take-off climb in both cases. The key issue, however, was that Boeing had concealed the system’s existence from the FAA and other regulators, as well as airlines. This meant the MCAS was not referenced in any of the aircraft documents or even training manuals, because it was reportedly a concern for Boeing that disclosing a new system could lead to certification delays and might reduce the flight deck commonality of the MAX aircraft compared to previous 737 jets, thus becoming less attractive to airlines due to additional crew-training expenses….

Riot police have been deployed to confront the increasingly violent protests.
